title: Disparate Conditional Prediction in Multiclass Classifiers

strengths: The paper addresses an important auditing problem: determining what aggregate label statistics imply about classifier accuracy and fairness when individual predictions or validation labels are unavailable. Formulating this as optimization over compatible confusion matrices is well motivated.

The baseline-mixture definition gives unfairness an explicit mathematical meaning and supports a useful monotonicity property under merging predicted labels. The binary reduction to finite candidates and one-dimensional searches is a substantive technical idea.

The experiments cover 410 binary classification tasks, multiclass Census and Natality problems, and several applications. The initialization ablations demonstrate improvements from greedy initialization plus local optimization, with matching upper and lower bounds in several cases. Algorithms and a code link aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The mixed accuracy–fairness guarantees have substantive mathematical inconsistencies. Section 7.1 defines its variables as mistake rates but applies τβ(a,b)=βη(a,b)+(1−β)(1−b), thereby penalizing accuracy instead of error. Equation (26) also omits the population weights from its error term. Moreover, Lemma 7.3 bounds the derivative of η while claiming a bound for τβ: a=0.2, b=0.4, c=0.1, d=0.2 gives the stated bound zero, although |ψ′|=0.2(1−β). These issues may be repairable, but the discrepancy calculation and Algorithm 2’s tolerance guarantee require corrected derivations and validation.

Section 7 claims that constrained error minimization is equivalent to selecting an appropriate discrepancy weight β. Weighted scalarization generally recovers only supported Pareto points, and the necessary convexity or other structural justification is absent. Consequently, the interpretation of Figures 7–9 as the complete best-possible tradeoff requires additional proof; connecting finitely sampled minimizers does not establish a certified frontier.

The rare-disease justification for the unfairness measure is overstated. Choosing the identity confusion matrix as the baseline immediately gives unfairness ≤ error. For equally weighted groups with disease prevalence p, zero false positives, and false-negative rates 0.1 and 0.2, the measure is p/18, which vanishes as the disease becomes rare despite the twofold disparity. This does not invalidate the definition, but contradicts the claimed necessarily high unfairness in such cases and weakens its asserted advantage over absolute-difference measures.

The central multiclass experiment with unknown confusion matrices provides insufficient evidence about inference quality. Tables 5–8 report local-search upper bounds on minimum possible unfairness, which cannot establish how much unfairness the aggregates compel. Table 5’s six-label decision tree has an upper bound of 3.20% despite actual unfairness of 0.77%, demonstrating a substantial optimization gap. Corresponding lower bounds, runtime measurements, and initialization/tolerance sensitivity are needed. Trends in Figure 12’s upper bounds alone cannot establish trends in underlying unfairness.

The application conclusions depend on insufficiently examined population and uncertainty assumptions. For example, statewide cancer incidence is combined with Bing-user prediction rates without establishing matching populations or time horizons. Section 4 briefly mentions interval constraints, but the full inference procedures lack uncertainty calibration. The clipping and marginal smoothing in Sections 6.2.2 and 7.2 also alter the inference problem without a bound relating the reported certificates to the original inputs.

Originality relative to the authors’ prior work is difficult to assess. The manuscript explicitly calls itself an extension of Sabato and Yom-Tov (ICML 2020), but does not clearly identify which definitions, binary results, algorithms, and experiments are inherited and which contributions are new. This distinction is especially important when assessing the significance of the multiclass extension.

The mixture-based unfairness measure has a precise statistical definition. Its formulation through a shared baseline confusion matrix and its monotonicity under label coarsening provide useful conceptual structure.
The binary finite-candidate reduction is insightful, and the multiclass experiments with known confusion matrices provide useful comparisons of initialization and local optimization methods.
The experiments span several applications and include validation against individual-level Census data. The manuscript provides substantial derivations and links implementation and experiment code.
weaknesses: The printed optimization objectives are inconsistent with the defined discrepancy. Section 7.1 switches to false-positive and false-negative rates but retains τβ(a,b)=βη(a,b)+(1−β)(1−b), thereby penalizing accuracy instead of error. For identical groups with true and predicted positive proportions of 1/4 and β=1/2, a perfect fair classifier is feasible, yet the printed objective has minimum 1/4 rather than zero. Equations (26) and (29) also omit the population weights w_gπ_g^y from the error term. These may be transcription errors, but they affect the central optimization problems; the implementation and affected results need reconciliation and verification.

Lemma 7.3 is false as stated because its derivative bound omits the error component of τβ. For β=1/2, a=b=0.4 and c=d=0.2, η(a+bx,c+dx)=1/2 throughout x∈(0,1), so |ψ′(x)|=0.1, whereas the stated bound is zero. Consequently, the Lipschitz-based tolerance guarantee for ArgMin1D does not follow from the supplied proof.

Section 7 asserts equivalence between optimizing error under an unfairness constraint and selecting a weighted-sum parameter β. Such equivalence requires additional justification: weighted scalarization generally recovers only supported Pareto points, and no suitable convexity or strong-duality result is established here. The resulting curves can provide lower bounds without necessarily describing every best feasible tradeoff.

The practical guarantees require better treatment of uncertain and mismatched statistics. The cancer-query application combines Bing-user prediction rates with general-population cancer incidence without establishing that these describe the same target population and outcome window. Sections 6.2.2 and 7.2 also perturb confusion matrices or prediction proportions for numerical stability without bounding the resulting change in the reported certificates. The brief suggestion to incorporate uncertainty into the fair-classifier LP does not resolve these issues for the main nonlinear procedures.

The multiclass aggregate-data evaluation does not establish approximation quality. Tables 5–8 primarily report upper bounds on minimum unfairness; comparing these with an existing classifier’s unfairness does not measure their distance from the minimum. The six-label decision-tree example returns 3.20% although the classifier’s unfairness is 0.77%, demonstrating a substantial optimization gap. Paired lower bounds or globally solved small instances are needed, alongside evaluation for β<1 and runtime/tolerance measurements. Interpreting changes in the UK-election upper bounds as changes in minimum unfairness is consequently premature.

The claimed advantage under extreme class imbalance is overstated. The measure weights conditional disparities by label prevalence. With two equally sized groups, common disease prevalence ε, zero false-positive rates, and false-negative rates 0.1 and 0.2, unfairness equals ε/18 and vanishes as the disease becomes rare. This behavior is consistent with measuring population mass, but the manuscript should acknowledge it when asserting that a twofold rare-disease diagnostic disparity produces high unfairness.

Originality relative to the authors’ ICML 2020 paper is insufficiently delineated. Calling this an extended version does not identify which definitions, theoretical results, algorithms, and experiments are new.
